summary: Describes an RTCP Extended Report block, developed by BT, that reports packet transport parameters. It was written so the block type could be registered with IANA. The document does not standardize the report block. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This describes one extra measurement form a phone company made up for checking call quality. It is written down so that the name is reserved.

questions: how does xnq measure call quality
subtitle: A call quality report block for measuring packet delay variation and network degradation.

tldr.problem: RTP calls need metrics beyond standard RTCP packet loss and delay to measure network quality, particularly packet delay variation and jitter buffer behavior.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5093 defines an RTCP Extended Reports (XR) block type 8 containing nine metrics: maximum packet delay variation, delay range, cumulative delay variation, jitter buffer events, and error/severely-errored second counters.
tldr.outcome: BT registered this block type for pre-standards use in their network but did not standardize it for general use. Work in progress on RTCP HR is expected to supersede these metrics.

today: RFC 5093 is Informational. It documents a vendor-specific RTCP XR block developed by BT for pre-standards use in their network. The IANA registry of RTCP XR block types includes block type 8 with reference to this RFC, but the block is not recommended for general use. Modern call quality monitoring typically uses other standardized metrics.

sections.title: Extending RTCP for Better Metrics
sections.content:
The Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) uses RTCP to send feedback from receivers to senders about call quality. Standard RTCP reports packet loss and roundtrip delay, but this information is not enough to diagnose network problems.

BT (the UK telecommunications company) developed a set of metrics called XNQ (eXtended Network Quality) to measure additional aspects of call quality. These metrics supplement standard RTCP by reporting packet delay variation (jitter), jitter buffer events, and error statistics. RFC 5093 documents the XNQ metrics and defines how to send them inside an RTCP Extended Reports block so the block type can be registered with IANA. The RFC explicitly states that this block type does not constitute a standard; it is documented for BT's pre-standards use only.
sections.plainLanguage: RTCP is how one side of a call tells the other side the quality is bad. But RTCP only counts lost packets. BT invented extra measurements to detect when the network is jittery or when the receiver's buffer has to adapt. This document describes those measurements.

sections.title: The Nine XNQ Metrics
sections.content:
The XNQ report block contains nine metrics, each measured as an unsigned integer. vmaxdiff (16 bits) is the largest variation in packet delay seen within a single RTCP measurement cycle. vrange (16 bits) is the difference between the longest and shortest delay over the lifetime of the connection. Both are measured in RTP timestamp units.

vsum (32 bits) is the sum of per-cycle delay differences accumulated over all RTCP cycles. c (16 bits) is the count of cycles over which vsum was accumulated. Together, vsum and c allow calculation of average jitter per cycle.

jbevents (16 bits) counts adaptation events in the jitter buffer, such as when the receiver plays out incorrect samples, repeats samples, or skips samples sent by the transmitter. tdegnet (24 bits) and tdegjit (24 bits) are total sample periods of degradation caused by network loss or late delivery, and by jitter buffer adaptation, respectively.

es (24 bits) counts cumulative seconds affected by unavailable packet events ('errored seconds'). ses (24 bits) counts severely errored seconds where a severe proportion of packets were unavailable. For all metrics, a reserved 0xFFFFFF value indicates an over-range measurement.
sections.plainLanguage: The nine numbers measure: biggest jitter in one cycle, biggest jitter ever, total jitter, how many cycles, jitter buffer fixes, seconds damaged by network loss, seconds damaged by buffer fixes, bad seconds, and really bad seconds.

sections.title: RTCP XR Block Format
sections.content:
The XNQ report block fits inside an RTCP XR message as defined by RFC 3611. Each report is exactly 32 bytes: an 8-byte header and an 8-word (32-byte) data block.

The header contains a block type field set to 8, a reserved field for future use (must be zero), and the block length set to 8 (the number of 32-bit words in the block).

The data block holds begin_seq and end_seq sequence numbers identifying the RTP packets covered by the report, followed by the nine metrics: vmaxdiff, vrange, vsum, c, jbevents, tdegnet, tdegjit, es, and ses. Each metric is stored in network byte order as an unsigned integer of the specified width.
sections.plainLanguage: The XNQ report is a fixed-size message 32 bytes long. It has a header saying 'this is block type 8', and then nine numbers in a row.

sections.title: Security and Limitations
sections.content:
RFC 5093 notes that the XNQ block introduces no new security considerations beyond those in RFC 3611 (RTCP XR). The block does not provide per-packet statistics, so the confidentiality risk of exposing individual packet information is avoided. XNQ reports are small, so they do not pose the denial-of-service risk that large RTCP reports could cause.

The RFC emphasizes that this specification does not standardize XNQ for use outside BT's network. Work in progress at the time on RTCP HR (High Resolution) was expected to obsolete these metrics with more comprehensive and standardized quality reporting mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: XNQ reports do not leak information about individual packets, and they are small, so they do not create security problems. But this block type is only for BT's own network, not for general use.
